title: Judge: Nursing home fired worker who complained of supply shortages
description: A caregiver at an Iowa nursing home was fired after expressing concern with her employer’s alleged refusal to purchase supplies for residents, an Iowa judge has found. State records show Renee Arnold worked for the Azria Health Prairie Ridge nursing home in Mediapolis from June 1990 through December 2025, when she was fired. She subsequently […]
text:
The Azria Health Prairie Ridge nursing home and assisted living facility in Mediapolis, Iowa. (Photo via Google Earth)A caregiver at an Iowa nursing home was fired after expressing concern with her employer’s alleged refusal to purchase supplies for residents, an Iowa judge has found.
State records show Renee Arnold worked for the Azria Health Prairie Ridge nursing home in Mediapolis from June 1990 through December 2025, when she was fired. She subsequently applied for unemployment benefits, which the home challenged, leading to a recent hearing before Administrative Law Judge Jasmina Sarajlija.
In her findings of fact in the case, Sarajlija concluded that Arnold had been told by the home’s administrator, Ashley Ames, that she was “not to tell staff that corporate would not let her order supplies because they were over budget.” In August 2025, Arnold was given a written warning after she allegedly responded to an aide’s request for briefs for a resident by stating, “Placed the order, they will be here on Wednesday. That’s the best I can do.”
Arnold received another warning days later when she allegedly failed to properly report an incident of a resident choking and an incident involving a resident-on-resident altercation. She was fired in December 2025.
Based on hearing testimony, Sarajlija concluded that when Arnold placed an order for supplies, “she would receive communication from corporate that her order was over the allotted budget. For instance, claimant would order seven boxes of Saltine crackers and corporate would reduce her order to five boxes due to the imposed corporate budget.”
Arnold “routinely” talked to Ames about the issue, Sarajlija found, and Ames would then speak to corporate. “However, the budget issue went unresolved,” Sarajlija found. “As recently as two weeks before her discharge, claimant talked to her supervisor that the system was not working and that she had on occasion used her own money to purchase some supplies.”
In ruling that Arnold was entitled to unemployment benefits, Sarajlija stated that she found Arnold’s “version of events to be more credible than the employer’s recollection of those events,” noting that Azria Health “did not present a witness with direct knowledge of the situation to dispute (Arnold’s) testimony.”
Sarajlija concluded that Arnold “spoke to her supervisor, repeatedly, to keep her informed of the challenges when trying to order enough supplies while corporate stopped or reduced the order due to budget caps.”
Iowa Capital Dispatch was unable to reach Arnold for comment.
Other Iowans whose unemployment cases recently went before a judge include:
— Candy Canida, a registered nurse who worked for River Hills Village care center in Keokuk from November 2025 through early December 2025 when she was fired. According to the findings of the judge in her unemployment case, Canida was in training, job-shadowing another registered nurse, on Nov. 28, 2025, when she gave a resident the wrong medication and failed to catch the error. On Dec. 1, 2025, she gave a different resident of the home the wrong medication according to state records.
Canida alleged the nurse she was job-shadowing had gathered the medications and directed her as to which resident to give the drugs – an allegation the facility denied. The judge in the case found Canida’s testimony more persuasive than that of the employer and awarded her unemployment benefits.
— Austin Taylor, who, from April 2025 through December 2025 worked as a technician for a medical-equipment provider in Des Moines called AdaptHealth. According to the findings of the judge in Taylor’s unemployment case, Taylor was working on Dec. 18, 2025, when he went to a hospice facility where the staff reported Taylor appeared to be impaired and they did not feel it was safe to leave him alone with patients. Later that day, two AdaptHealth employees informed Taylor’s supervisor, Kellie Phipps, that Taylor was acting strange, and was pacing, sweating, making strange mouth gestures and pulling his hair.
According to the judge’s findings, Phipps later reported that when she then spoke to Taylor in her office, he was “amped up,” sweating profusely, could not sit still, and his eyes were darting back and forth. Phipps reported that Taylor agreed he needed to seek immediate medical attention, but refused to let her drive him to the hospital for testing. Taylor then ran from the office, got into his car and drove away, prompting Phipps to notify the police, according to state records. Taylor was then fired for violating the company’s policies related to drug-testing in cases of reasonable suspicion of impairment. He was denied unemployment benefits.
— Jeremey Gettemy, who, from December 2025 through mid-January 2026, worked as a full-time addiction technician for Bridges of Iowa, an addiction rehabilitation center in Des Moines. As part of his job, Gettemy worked at the Polk County Jail. Bridges of Iowa alleged Gettemy had several issues related to attendance such as showing up for work late or not showing up at all. The organization also alleged Gettemy lied about the death of his father, who was still alive when Gettemy sought time off for bereavement. His employer also alleged Gettemy had difficulty collecting the correct amounts of urine from individuals to conduct testing and had trouble maintaining client confidentiality. He was denied unemployment benefits.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: All the ways, big and little, Maine lawmakers tried to alleviate the housing crisis this session
description: Maine’s housing crisis was front of mind for state lawmakers this session, as they allocated more funding to housing programs and pushed for technical fixes to incentivize construction.  Erik Jorgensen, senior director of government relations and communications at the Maine State Housing Authority, said activity this session shows that housing remains a high[...]
text:
Mainers rally for more funding for housing initiatives in Augusta on March 26, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Maine’s housing crisis was front of mind for state lawmakers this session, as they allocated more funding to housing programs and pushed for technical fixes to incentivize construction. 
Erik Jorgensen, senior director of government relations and communications at the Maine State Housing Authority, said activity this session shows that housing remains a high priority for Maine legislators. 
“I think that really represents the continuation of the Legislature’s commitment and the administration’s commitment to housing,” Jorgensen said. “Even when some of the budgets have gotten tighter, they’ve still found ways of finding funding, and we’re really, really grateful for that.”
A 2023 study found that Maine needs an additional 38,500 housing units of varying price points and sizes to meet the current demand, and at least 84,000 homes by 2030. 
The MaineHousing Housing Outlook Report, released in January, found that affordability remains a central and worsening issue in the state, and despite strong affordable housing production, the overall housing supply is still constrained. 
“We’re a very desirable place, and now, the factors that used to keep people from living here — for better or for worse — are gone,” Jorgensen said of the state’s growth. “I think we’ve benefited from some of this, no question. But at the same time, there’s definitely a lot of demand now for housing.”
The increasing demand has driven up the cost of housing in Maine, making it harder for residents to stay in their homes and more difficult for people experiencing homelessness to get into housing. And all of that puts more pressure on Maine’s shelter system, said Terence Miller, advocacy director at Preble Street.
“The lack of housing, lack of affordable housing, the lack of viable situations for people to go into, create this perennial need for shelters and their existence,” Miller said.
Although shelters also saw more funding this year, Miller said like much of Maine’s housing issues, the challenge remains.
“We’re hoping that there is more acknowledgement, recognition for what shelters do within this housing continuum, but also the vital role they play in the placement and identifying of housing solutions for the most vulnerable in our society,” Miller said.
As a quasi-state agency, MaineHousing works on affordable housing around the state, with programs to subsidize affordable housing construction, and help residents buy, rent, heat and repair their homes. 
Jorgensen said that the state’s work to boost affordable housing programs has made a dent in the issue, but that is only part of Maine’s housing problem.
“We can subsidize things till the cows come home, but in the end, we’re a part of the picture,” Jorgensen said. “We’re just a part of it.”
At the same time, the private housing sector can be more difficult for the state government to stimulate. Jorgensen said it will likely require a broader debate about Maine’s zoning codes, a hot-button issue that often runs into pushback over local control.
And those zoning reforms are an area that didn’t get as much attention this session.
“I think the policy solutions are harder, probably than just finding funding,” Jorgensen said. “Finding funding is hard,” Jorgensen said, “but we really need to work on zoning stuff more.”
Supplemental budget
The bulk of housing activity this session was included in the supplemental budget passed by the Democratic majority.
In total, it includes roughly $74 million for housing programs, including $37.5 million for housing production through the state’s rural affordable rental program, the 4% Low Income Housing Tax Credit Program, the affordable home ownership program and others.
“In any other world than housing, it would be … a ton of money,” Jorgensen said. But with the rising cost of construction and materials, he said the needs are still significant.
Jorgensen pointed to the eviction prevention program as another key initiative included in the budget, receiving $11 million in one-time funding.
“Eviction prevention is important too, because once someone gets evicted, it’s so much harder for them after that time to rent up again,” Jorgensen said.
Lawmakers also considered bond proposals for affordable housing and workforce housing, but they ultimately saw little support.
A large bond package that included $20 million for the rural affordable housing rental program and a pilot program supporting the construction of new homes in mobile home parks made it through initial votes in the Senate and House of Representatives.
But that bill failed to get the necessary two-thirds majority for enactment. It was later amended to only include an agriculture bond, but even that failed to get enacted before the Legislature adjourned.
Emergency shelters
Another key area of Maine’s housing support system are the state’s 37 emergency shelters, which serve people experiencing homelessness and connect them with housing support programs and other key services.
But the shelters have struggled for years with rising costs and low reimbursement rates from the state and federal government.
Miller with Preble Street said Maine has more than 2,000 homeless individuals, while the 37 emergency shelters have roughly 1,200 beds.
“There is still a gap, not only with the beds, but with ongoing funding,” Miller said.
In this session’s supplemental budget, the annual appropriation for emergency shelters got a long-awaited $1.5 million increase, bringing it to a total of $4 million.
“This is the first increase since 2016, about 10 years, that emergency shelter operation has seen on a permanent, ongoing, sustainable basis,” Miller said.
And while that is a substantial improvement, Miller said, it falls short of the $5 million increase the shelters were seeking to compensate for the estimated $7.5 million a year needed to support Maine’s needs.
Miller said he is grateful for the bipartisan support, but “there’s still a significant gap in sustainable ongoing funding that we will be going back to the 133rd Legislature to rectify.”
The shelters got some further support through one-time funding, with another $3.25 million included in the budget, and LD 2124, which was signed into law last month, providing another $1 million from the real estate transfer tax.
While the Legislature has worked to fund affordable housing programs in recent years, Miller noted that those new units often take years to get constructed and ready for residents — and in that wait time, emergency shelters are a key support for people.
“And so there’s a gap here that we really need to address and pay attention to, so that more people do not fall into homelessness,” Miller said.
Technical changes
Gov. Janet Mills also signed into law a number of technical changes meant to encourage housing development across the state.
That includes legislation to extend the state’s affordable housing tax credit until 2036 and another to amend the definition of “subdivision.”
Another bill continues the Legislature’s effort to adjust zoning across Maine to encourage more housing development. In 2022, lawmakers passed a major law that eliminated single-family zoning restrictions and made it easier to build accessory dwelling units. This session, they made several tweaks to the 2022 provision, clarifying changes to height requirements, fire suppression and sewer systems.
But it’s hard to say if more changes will be needed and how much of a difference it will make in the long run.
Also signed into law is a measure designed to make manufactured and tiny homes more affordable by allowing those who own such structures on leased land to reclassify the building as real estate. That allows the owner to access the mortgage market, which has more consumer protections, longer loan terms and generally lower interest rates. Another bill to support industrialized housing failed to secure funding, leaving it to die on the appropriations table as the Legislature adjourned. 
Under a new law, MaineHousing will have a higher bonding cap of $4 million. The change has no financial impacts on the state, but allows the housing authority to borrow against itself to a higher amount.
MaineHousing sells bonds, and then uses those funds to purchase first-time homebuyer mortgages and to issue construction loans. Jorgenson said it’s an important law for the organization to keep momentum going on a range of housing programs.
“This is what I would describe as a housekeeping bill,” he said. “But it was the kind of bill that if it didn’t pass, it would be a lot more than a messy house.”
With the rise in construction costs and general inflation, Jorgenson said the housing authority is not spending the bond funds on more projects, but rather those project costs continue to rise.
Another law from the session expands the authority’s ability to make construction loans.
“So you know, our goal isn’t to try to undercut all the commercial banks, but it’s another tool we have for circumstances where it makes sense to do construction lending,” Jorgensen said.
Finally, the Legislature passed a bill last year to try and discourage large out-of-state companies from buying mobile home parks by creating an additional fee for those companies on the purchase. A new law passed this year is meant to refine how those buyers are assessed and who gets charged that fee.
Not funded
But many additional proposals that won the support of legislators failed to secure funding either in the supplemental budget or through the appropriations table, where bills vie for remaining resources, leaving them dead on adjournment. 
That includes a measure that would have allocated $5 million in ongoing funding to convert vacant school buildings into housing.
“Schools have been proven to be really good places to have housing, but they’re not always easy to develop,” Jorgensen explained. “They have various building issues, sometimes all asbestos, sometimes other things that have to be dealt with that most developers don’t want to take on.”
The failed bill sought to address the problem by having the Maine Redevelopment Land Bank Authority offer technical support to developers, and use funding to start some work on the buildings and get them ready for developers to build housing.
Another that attempted to expand the sales tax exemption for manufactured homes — seeking to increase the cap from 50% of the sale price to 75% — died because it was left unfunded.
There were also several proposals that were watered down into a study of the underlying issue, and still ultimately failed to secure funding.
That includes a bill that originally sought to create a statewide housing resolution board — essentially an appeals board for zoning matters.
The idea was to create an appeals process for situations when a developer is meeting all local written requirements, but still runs into local pushback, the so-called ‘not in my backyard,’ or NIMBY roadblocks. The statewide board would evaluate if a developer has met the letter of the local ordinance, and ensure the city or town follows its own rules.
“So if you follow all the rules, you do it right, but the town still blocks it, this is a way of getting a chance to go up and have it overridden and still be able to build it,” Jorgensen said.
But the bill ran into pushback, as opponents cited concerns about local control for municipalities.
It was amended to instead create the Commission to Study Pathways to Increase Efficiency in Resolving Legal Disputes Involving Housing Development Projects to study the issue. But like many other proposals this session, the study was left unfunded and died on the study table. 
Another bill originally sought to ban housing discrimination based on a renter’s source of income or use of rental vouchers. But the measure was eventually reduced to a study on tenant-landlord relationships and ways to increase the use of housing vouchers — and still left unfunded.
And although Mills signed into law a measure to create a middle income housing support program, it faces an unlikely future because it was not given sufficient funds to meaningfully launch the program.
The program will offer rental assistance to households making up to 120% of the area median income, and homeownership options for households making up to 180% of the area median income.
But while the law establishes the program and creates a fund for it, lawmakers allocated just $500, the minimum to establish the fund, instead of the original allocation of $10 million for the program in Mills’ budget proposal.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: FBI raids Sen. Louise Lucas’ Portsmouth office, cannabis business
description: Federal agents on Wednesday morning raided the Portsmouth office of state Sen. Louise Lucas, one of Virginia’s most powerful Democratic lawmakers, a representative of the Federal Bureau of Investigations confirmed Wednesday, after multiple news outlets reported an extensive law enforcement operation that included FBI agents, SWAT teams and court-authorized s[...]
text:
State Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, on the Senate floor at the Virginia Capitol in Richmond. Federal agents on Wednesday raided Lucas’ Portsmouth office and adjacent cannabis business as part of a court-authorized FBI search operation. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Federal agents on Wednesday morning raided the Portsmouth office of state Sen. Louise Lucas, one of Virginia’s most powerful Democratic lawmakers, a representative of the Federal Bureau of Investigations confirmed Wednesday, after multiple news outlets reported an extensive law enforcement operation that included FBI agents, SWAT teams and court-authorized searches tied to several locations across the commonwealth.











FBI spokeswoman Cassandra Temple told The Mercury at the scene: “We are conducting court-authorized law enforcement activity today.” She wouldn’t confirm or answer any other questions, including whether anyone had been arrested.











Fox News, who was first to report the news, said the FBI executed search warrants at several sites, including Lucas’ legislative office in Portsmouth. Staffers inside the building were ordered outside and were not allowed to re-enter as agents searched the premises. Witnesses saw federal agents carrying boxes out of the building.
Adjacent to Lucas’ office is The Cannabis Outlet, a hemp- and cannabis related retail business linked to the longtime state senator. Fox News reported that SWAT teams arrived there with weapons drawn and ordered everyone inside to exit the building with their hands up. At least three people were reportedly placed in handcuffs and taken into custody.
Lucas arrived at the scene shortly after the raid began. When asked by a reporter what the federal action was about, she replied that she had no idea. 
The FBI field office in Norfolk did not immediately respond Wednesday morning to questions from The Mercury about the nature of the investigation or whether charges had been filed. Lucas also did not immediately respond to requests for comment. 
The scope of the investigation sent shockwaves through Virginia political circles because of Lucas’ outsized role in state government and Democratic politics. 
U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott, D-Newport News, whose district includes Portsmouth, was among the first elected officials to publicly respond to the raid, arguing the federal action comes amid what he described as President Donald Trump’s attacks on political opponents. 
“While we await the full facts of the investigation, it must be acknowledged that this FBI raid occurs in the broader context of President Trump’s repeated abuse of the Department of Justice to target his perceived political opponents,” Scott said in an emailed statement. 
He also noted the raid came roughly two weeks after Lucas helped lead Virginia’s redistricting referendum effort, which Democrats hailed as a rejection of Trump-backed attempts to influence GOP states to redraw their congressional maps ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. 
Scott added that “like all Americans, Senator Lucas has a right to due process and a presumption of innocence.” 
House Speaker Don Scott, D-Portsmouth, urged caution as details about the federal investigation remained unclear. He too noted that Lucas had not been charged with a crime. 
“Let’s start with this: Senator L. Louise Lucas has not been charged with anything,” Scott said in a statement. He added that, given what he described as the politicization of the Trump administration’s Justice Department and FBI, “people should take this with a grain of salt and allow the facts to come out before jumping to conclusions.” 
Scott also questioned how Fox News appeared to be positioned at the scene early in the operation and said Virginians deserve more transparency about the raid. 
“At this point we simply do not know what this ultimately means,” he said. “Right now, there is far more theatrics and speculation than actual information available to the public.”
The Lucas Professional Center in Portsmouth, where the FBI conducted a raid of Sen. Louise Lucas’ legislative office and nearby cannabis shop. Vehicles blocked off the entrance to the parking lot. (Photo by Roger Chesley/Virginia Mercury)
Lucas, 82, has served in the Virginia Senate since 1992 and currently serves as the chamber’s president pro tempore, making her one of the highest ranking members of the General Assembly. A Democrat from Portsmouth, she has long been one of the legislature’s most influential and combative political figures, particularly on budget and fiscal matters. 
She also chairs the powerful Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee, placing her at the center of this year’s contentious intraparty budget negotiations.
In recent months, Lucas has pushed aggressively to end or scale back Virginia’s lucrative sales and use tax exemptions for data centers, arguing the incentives have become too costly for the state and place growing strain on Virginia’s electric grid and infrastructure. 
House Democrats and Gov. Abigail Spanberger have resisted the effort, creating a major impasse that has delayed completion of the state budget.
Lucas has also played a leading role in Virginia’s controversial redistricting referendum approved by voters last month. She was among the key Democratic architects behind the constitutional amendment effort, which would allow Virginia to redraw congressional maps mid-decade under certain political conditions.
The amendment remains in legal limbo while under review by the Supreme Court of Virginia following a court challenge questioning whether lawmakers properly followed constitutional procedures before placing the measure on the ballot.
Beyond her legislative work, Lucas has also faced scrutiny tied to Virginia’s evolving cannabis laws. Virginia legalized simple possession of marijuana in 2021 through legislation Lucas co-sponsored. 
But a 2022 Virginia Mercury investigation found that cannabis-related products sold at The Cannabis Outlet contained levels of THC inconsistent with labeling and were being sold in a largely unregulated retail environment that existed before Virginia established a legal recreational cannabis marketplace.
At the time, laboratory testing commissioned by The Mercury found some products sold at the store exceeded advertised THC concentrations. The story put a spotlight on concerns about Virginia’s loosely regulated hemp and cannabis market following legalization of marijuana possession but before creation of a fully regulated retail sales system, which is now before Spanberger.
As of  Wednesday afternoon, federal authorities had not publicly indicated whether the raids were connected to Lucas’ cannabis business, her legislative activities or another matter entirely.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: School choice, vouchers fuel nearly $3M spending spree in WV statehouse races from 3 outside groups
description: School choice is driving the avalanche of money spent this primary election season to impact West Virginia Statehouse races. Much of the money is coming from out-of-state donors. Early voting is underway in what has been a contentious and abnormally expensive mid-term election season in the Mountain State.  The Sugar Maple Political Action Committee, School[...]
text:
A child holds up a poster in support of the Hope Scholarship, West Virginia’s education voucher program, during a House Finance Committee meeting at the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, on Feb. 20, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)School choice is driving the avalanche of money spent this primary election season to impact West Virginia Statehouse races. Much of the money is coming from out-of-state donors.
Early voting is underway in what has been a contentious and abnormally expensive mid-term election season in the Mountain State. 
The Sugar Maple Political Action Committee, School Freedom Fund and Americans for Prosperity are slated to be the highest spenders this cycle, pouring around $3 million into races in hopes of influencing voters, particularly on the issue of school choice. 
“School choice is a litmus test for Republicans,” said Jason Huffman, state director for West Virginia’s chapter of Americans for Prosperity. The group is backing candidates who will defend the state’s school choice laws, he said.
All 100 House of Delegates seats and 19 Senate seats are on ballots across West Virginia.
The majority of West Virginia students attend public schools.
The focus on school choice in Statehouse races comes as West Virginia is experiencing a wave of public school closures and teacher and staff reductions. Schools’ financial problems are largely tied to the state’s population decline. Many school districts also point to the state’s school voucher program, the Hope Scholarship, as a contributor to dire finances. 
Del. Hollis Lewis, D-Kanawha (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Hollis Lewis, D-Kanawha, who is running unopposed for reelection, is concerned about what school choice expansion could look like in West Virginia. 
“I don’t know how much more we can push the line. It’s definitely scary to think about what’s next,” Lewis said. “I think when we look at the state of public education, a lot of resources and different things could be going to solve those issues.”
Sugar Maple PAC has contributed heavily this campaign cycle, raising more than $1.2 million to spend in West Virginia’s legislative races, and it’s spent much of it. 
The group, raking in out-of-state funds, has ties to Gov. Patrick Morrisey. The Republican governor has made school choice and promoting the Hope Scholarship a hallmark issue of his tenure.
MetroNews reporter Brad McElhinny pointed out that several of the PAC’s donors are tied to the school choice movement. Billionaire and Pennsylvania resident Jeff Yass, who has advocated for school vouchers across the country, has poured $450,000 into the Sugar Maple PAC in the last few months. 
“The money is not local,” said Del Vernon Criss, R-Wood, whose House race has been central in pro-school choice spending. “(School choice) is an issue that the governor’s wife has picked and that she has promoted through these acts, and she’s directed the governor to get on board with this.”
A spokesperson for the governor didn’t return a request for comment from Denise Morrisey by the time this article was published.
School Freedom Fund, based in Washington, D.C., dropped around $200,000 into supporting or opposing West Virginia Senate and House candidates just this week in a spending report filed Tuesday. 
Overall, they’ve spent more than $900,000.
The group is connected to Club for Growth and pushes for school voucher programs nationwide.
The School Freedom Fund didn’t reply to an inquiry for this story.
House Finance Chairman Vernon Criss, R-Wood, stands before the committee on Feb. 20, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
School choice at center of high-profile House race in Wood County
AFP is a national conservative advocacy organization founded by David and Charles Koch. 
Huffman said AFP expects to spend close to $1 million this primary season; typically, he said, they’ d spend around $600,000 to $700,000. 
The group’s West Virginia chapter has spent more than $750,000 this primary season as of Wednesday, according to campaign finance reports. They’ve knocked on more than 25,000 doors statewide ahead of Election Day. 
AFP is focused on candidates who support school choice, income tax cuts and a repeal of West Virginia’s certificate of need health care laws, Huffman explained.
“We lack a policy majority in the House, and that was very evident based on the attacks on school choice,” he said.
They’re involved in a high-profile House race in Wood County, where AFP is pushing to oust Criss. He is being challenged by Republican Charles Hartzog. 
Criss holds the powerful position of House Finance Chair, overseeing lawmakers’ funding for state agencies, the governor’s initiatives and more. He voted yes on legislation that created the Hope Scholarship in 2021.
“I’m all in favor of the program,” Criss said when reached by phone on Tuesday.
A recent study, paid for by the House, recommended that West Virginia put some restrictions on the broad Hope Scholarship school voucher program in an effort to improve public education funding in the state. The Hope Scholarship provides roughly $5,200 per student to use for private school tuition, homeschool supplies, extracurricular activities and more. 
Much of AFP’s attacks on Criss this primary season have centered on a bill that originated earlier this year in his House Finance Committee to put some guardrails on the Hope Scholarship. Proposed changes included banning the use of Hope funds at out-of-state schools.
The measure was in an effort to reduce the voucher program’s nearly $300 million price tag. The cost of the program has soared from $9 million in its first year, and the program opens up to all students this upcoming school year, leading to its massive price increase.
The House Finance Committee, ultimately, slashed most of the proposed changes, opting to change only when the voucher amount is disbursed to families or directly to private schools. The legislation didn’t impact how students use the program or reduce the price tag. 
“We had various ideas that we talked about in our private caucus, with the entire caucus and with the finance committee. We eliminated all the other options except the payment program,” Criss said. “That seemed to be palatable for everybody, because they understood the cash flow problem that the two payments made during the beginning of the fiscal year.”
Wood County students have one of the highest rates of use of the Hope Scholarship in the state, according to program data, with 607 students using it during the 2024-25 school year. There are multiple private religious schools in the area.
Criss said that school choice isn’t an issue typically brought up by his constituents. 
While lawmakers didn’t make any change to parents’ use of the Hope Scholarship, Huffman pointed to the original bill in Criss’ committee as the reason why they’ve backed his primary opponent. Mailers from AFP said that Criss “attacked school choice.”
“He had an originating bill that came out of his committee that would have kicked thousands of kids out of the Hope Scholarship, and that is why we are trying to elect a more principled leader in that district to represent people,” Huffman said. 
Hartzog said in a text message that he was running for the House “because we need a real conservative in the 12th District.”
“I will always support and defend the Hope Scholarship Program because I believe our kids deserve every opportunity to succeed and have an education built for them. Funding for our children’s education should always follow the student,” he said. “I believe West Virginia can become the best place to live, work and raise a family.”
Lewis said there needs to be guardrails on the Hope Scholarship. Several Democratic bills or amendments refining the program, including putting an income cap for parents, haven’t gotten traction in the GOP-heavy Legislature.
He wants to make sure that “the voucher program is actually going to families who need it, and not going to supplement families who could probably afford to pay out of pocket anyway.”
Early voting continues through May 9. Election day is May 12.

title: U.S. Interior Department announces Indian Country Violent Crime Task Force
description: The U.S. Department of the Interior on Tuesday announced its new Indian Country Violent Crime Task Force, which is tasked with targeting violent crime and drug activity in tribal communities.
text:
Geraldine Toya, the mother of Shawna Toya, makes a speech while surrounded by family members during a news conference on July 1, 2023, at the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center in Albuquerque. (Photo by Sharon Chischilly for Source NM)The U.S. Department of the Interior on Tuesday announced its new Indian Country Violent Crime Task Force, which is tasked with targeting violent crime and drug activity in tribal communities.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX
In an order titled “Honoring Our Commitment to Protecting Indian Country Communities,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote that he would continue to “honor America’s trust responsibility” to the nearly 2 million Native Americans and Alaska Natives served by the Bureau of Indian Affairs. 
“With American Indians and Alaska Natives facing alarming levels of violence across the country, protecting our children, elders, and the most vulnerable are key to protecting Tribal culture and living so that communities are safe from crime and drugs,” Burgum wrote. “Drug-related activity in Indian Country also continues to be a major contributor to violent crime and imposes serious health and economic hardships on our Tribal communities.”
The task force builds on previous Federal Bureau of Investigation work to investigate violent crimes in Indian Country. The FBI’s Operation Not Forgotten initiative sent federal agents to field offices in cities with large Indigenous populations, including Albuquerque, Denver and Phoenix.
Last year, the agency said the operation assisted with law enforcement investigations in more than 500 cases and led to “the recovery of 10 child victims, 52 arrests, and 25 indictments or judicial complaints.”
In his Tuesday announcement, Burgum said the Interior Department would deliver “decisive action to restore law and order, strengthen tribal sovereignty and equip tribal law enforcement with the tools they need to protect their communities.”
“Protecting communities in Indian Country is central to our trust responsibility, and under President Trump’s leadership, we are taking a zero-tolerance approach to violent crime, drug trafficking and those who prey on vulnerable populations,” he said in a statement.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs’ Missing and Murdered Unit, which former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland established in 2021, has agents across New Mexico and the U.S. who work with tribal, state and local law enforcement agencies to investigate crimes related to missing and murdered Indigenous people. Haaland previously told Source NM that, five years after launching the unit, there still exists an “an issue with data sharing.”
To that end, the New Mexico Department of Justice hosts a Missing and Murdered Indigenous Peoples portal, where residents can search for information about missing people or report a loved one missing. According to the department’s data dashboard, 201 Indigenous people have been reported missing in New Mexico.

The latter is 36 cents per gallon, meaning Hoosier motorists will save 59.3 cents a gallon for the next month. The 30-day tax suspensions, combined, are expected to […]
text:
An Indianapolis gas pump shows prices over $4 a gallon on Tuesday, April 7, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Gov. Mike Braun not only extended the suspension of the sales tax on gasoline another 30 days Wednesday — he paused the state gas tax, as well.
The latter is 36 cents per gallon, meaning Hoosier motorists will save 59.3 cents a gallon for the next month.
The 30-day tax suspensions, combined, are expected to cost state coffers $104 million and local units $52 million. Braun’s initial 30-day suspension of the 7% sales tax on gasoline came at a separate $50 million revenue cost.
“Making life more affordable for Hoosiers will always be my top priority,” Braun said Wednesday. “Suspending both the gas tax and excise tax gives Hoosiers meaningful relief for the next month.”
The current 30-day sales tax suspension was set to end May 8.
Braun said the energy emergency will give Hoosiers a 12.4% discount on the average price of gasoline in Indiana.
When Braun took action in April, the average cost for a gallon of gas in Indiana was $4.14, according to AAA. That price has now risen to $4.76.
Braun also announced Wednesday that he will increase the mileage reimbursement rate for state employees who utilize their own vehicles for work-related travel. Details on that increase will be shared once confirmed by the governor’s office.
This story will be updated.

text:
Maine’s Judicial Branch is warning residents of a new scam demanding payments for unpaid traffic violations, featuring a "final enforcement notice," shown here. (Photo courtesy of the Maine Judicial Branch)Maine’s Judicial Branch is warning residents of a new scam demanding payments for unpaid traffic violations.
The texts include an image of a “final enforcement notice” and demand payment for unpaid traffic violations, including failure to pay tolls, speeding tickets and parking violations.
The courts do not send enforcement notices or payment demands by text. If residents receive such a text, officials urge them to not click on any links or scan any QR codes in the message, and do not provide personal or payment information.
For questions about traffic violations, the Maine Violations Bureau’s helpline can be reached at 207-783-5422.
The latest wave of scam texts follows a similar trend flagged by the Maine Secretary of State’s Office in February.
Those texts warned of an “Important Reminder from the Maine DMV” and threatened consequences like vehicle registration and license suspension, late payments and legal proceedings for failing to pay for a supposed violation.
The office warned residents not to click on any links in the messages, and to be suspicious of any unsolicited text, email or call.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Community policing and federal immigration enforcement are different roles. Don’t mix them.
description: Across South Carolina, including in Orangeburg where I was born and raised, I’ve been hearing the same thing from folks I talk to every day. People feel uneasy. Not because they don’t believe in law and order, but because something about the way immigration enforcement is showing up in our communities doesn’t feel right. I […]
text:
Phil Ford testifies at a state House Judiciary subcommittee meeting Tuesday, Feb. 17, 2026, against legislation that would require law enforcement departments across South Carolina to sign an agreement with U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement under its 287(g) program. The bill cleared the House with an 84-26 vote April 2 in the Statehouse chamber. (Screenshot of SCETV legislative livestream)Across South Carolina, including in Orangeburg where I was born and raised, I’ve been hearing the same thing from folks I talk to every day. People feel uneasy. Not because they don’t believe in law and order, but because something about the way immigration enforcement is showing up in our communities doesn’t feel right.
I was at the Statehouse recently to voice my concerns, and what I said there is what I still believe now.
I am a proud resident of Orangeburg. I’ve lived there long enough to know what makes our community work. We look out for each other. We trust the people we elect. And we expect our local leaders to focus on the things that actually keep us safe.
In Orangeburg, we elected Sheriff Leroy Ravenell to do a job. That job is to protect our community, build trust with residents, and focus on the crimes that impact our daily lives. Violent
crime. Drug activity. Theft. The things that keep families up at night.
I trust him to do that job because I’ve seen how he shows up for our community.
This can also be said for every other community in our state. We elect the people we trust to keep us safe.
What I don’t trust is a system that starts blurring the lines between local law enforcement and federal immigration enforcement.
I said it before and I’ll say it again. Those are two different roles. If the federal government wants to enforce immigration law, that is their responsibility. Our local deputies are here to serve and
protect the people of our counties.
When we start mixing those responsibilities, we don’t get better outcomes. We get confusion, fear, and a breakdown of trust.
And that trust matters more than people realize.
When folks are afraid that any interaction with law enforcement could have immigration consequences, they start to pull back.
Victims of domestic violence hesitate to call for help. Witnesses think twice before speaking up. Families stop engaging with the very systems that are supposed to protect them.
I have had these conversations with my neighbors in Orangeburg. This isn’t a theory. This is real life. People are worried. And when people are worried, it doesn’t make our communities safer. It
makes it harder for law enforcement to do their jobs.
I also think about the practical side of it. Our local departments already have enough on their plate. Every hour spent trying to coordinate with federal immigration enforcement is an hour not
spent addressing the serious issues we’re dealing with right here at home.
As Congress spars over ICE, GOP legislators in SC advance bill requiring more cooperation

Every resource stretched thin is one less resource available to solve the problems we all agree need attention.
The folks making decisions from a distance don’t always see that. But we do.
We also can’t ignore the bigger picture. South Carolina has a long history when it comes to how systems of power affect different communities. That history didn’t just disappear. It still shapes
how people experience enforcement today.
When policies disproportionately impact certain groups, people notice. And they remember.
That’s why this moment matters.
This isn’t about being against the law. I believe in the law. I believe in accountability. But I also believe in fairness, in proportionality, and in treating people with basic human dignity.
Those values aren’t in conflict with public safety. They are what make public safety possible.
At the end of the day, this comes down to trust.
I trust the sheriff my community elected. I trust my neighbors to hold local leaders accountable.
And I trust that the people of South Carolina know what their communities need better than anyone else.
What I don’t trust is fear as a strategy.
We are better than that. We’ve seen what happens when fear drives policy, and it’s never led us anywhere good.
If we want stronger, safer communities, we have to build them on trust, not suspicion. On cooperation, not division.
South Carolina is full of good people who want the same thing. Safe neighborhoods. Strong families. A fair shot at a better life. That should be our focus.
When we lose sight of that, we don’t just fail one group of people. We weaken the very communities we’re trying to protect.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Officials select 10 counties for Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies pilot after halting program
description: In December 2024, Lakiyah Green, was an expectant mother who attended a parenting workshop at Bolivar County Library in Cleveland, Miss.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
The Mississippi State Department of Health’s home visitation program for high-risk infants and mothers will resume under a new model beginning in July and accept patients in 10 counties. 
The care management program called Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies previously served the entire state and stopped accepting patients in January. 
The selected counties are Adams, Alcorn, Forrest, George, Jones, Lauderdale, Neshoba, Oktibbeha, Panola and Pike, Greg Flynn, a department spokesperson, told Mississippi Today.
The Health Department does not have the resources to provide home visitation services to expectant mothers and their infants in all 82 counties, State Health Officer Dr. Dan Edney told reporters following an April 8 Board of Health meeting. The new pilot model aims to reduce infant mortality rates by focusing on counties that lack comparable services. 
“We identified 10 counties with no home visitation coverage, and we’re plugging into those 10 counties,” Edney said. 
The program serves high-risk mothers and infants by providing home visits, health education and referrals to wraparound services and benefits. Mothers qualify if they meet certain criteria, including chronic illness, substance use, unsafe living conditions or teen pregnancy. Infants may qualify if they were born prematurely, underweight or with medical complications. 
In August, the Department of Health declared a public health emergency in response to the state’s rising infant mortality rate — already the highest in the nation. In 2024, the state’s infant mortality rate was near twice the national average, and 323 infants died before their first birthday. Mississippi also has one of the nation’s highest maternal mortality rates.
Infant mortality disproportionately affects Black infants, who are three times more likely to die than white infants, according to the Health Department’s review of 2023 and 2024 data. In 2024, when Mississippi’s infant mortality rate reached a 10-year high, white infants experienced their lowest mortality rate in a decade.
Strengthening the Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies program is one of the agency’s key measures in its multi-pronged response to the crisis, according to its emergency declaration announcement. 
Edney told Mississippi Today in January that while Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies previously served moms and babies “wonderfully,” it failed to reduce infant and maternal mortality rates. 
The program’s new service area only includes one county — Panola — in the Mississippi Delta, a region of the state that suffers from some of the highest rates of infant mortality. Edney said Delta counties already receive similar services. 
“It may be surprising to many folks that the Delta counties are well covered with home visitation programs outside the Health Department,” Edney said. “So, we don’t have the resources to duplicate.”
Desiree Norwood is the program director for Plan A Health, a clinic that provides primary and reproductive health care to patients in the Delta regardless of their ability to pay at mobile clinics, telehealth appointments and a brick-and-mortar location in Louise. 
Plan A’s Healthy Families, Healthy Futures program supports families from pregnancy through early childhood by providing healthcare, resources and supplies to families with babies up to 18 months old. 
Desiree Norwood with Plan A prepares for patients to arrive at the Plan A clinic in Louise, Miss., Friday, July 1, 2022.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Norwood said Plan A previously referred clients to the Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies program. She said the program’s sudden pause in January took her by surprise and has been a loss for the Delta. 
While several programs in the region work to increase families’ access to prenatal and postpartum support, Norwood said the Health Department has access to additional resources and funding that can greatly help the region. 
“How can we afford to lose another program?” Norwood asked. “We need boots on the ground. We need all hands on deck.” 
Participants in areas that are no longer covered by the program will be referred to alternative home visitation services, such as Healthy Start and Medicaid services, Flynn previously told Mississippi Today. 
Flynn also said the program’s new version will rely on community health workers for home visitation rather than nurses. The model will use a team-based approach with registered nurses administering clinical oversight and health education, licensed social workers connecting patients to resources and community health workers providing regular support to participants. 
Officials have not clearly explained the policy decisions that resulted in the overhaul of the Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies program. Edney told Mississippi Today in January the change emerged after Mississippi Division of Medicaid transferred the primary financial responsibility for high-risk prenatal care to managed care, a shift the agency considered for a year. These private companies provide services to more than half of Medicaid beneficiaries
Mississippi Medicaid spokesperson Matt Westerfield did not respond to several requests for comment from Mississippi Today in January and February about the policy change. Flynn declined to provide additional details about the change and directed Mississippi Today’s questions to the Division of Medicaid. 
Many counties selected for the new pilot program had some of the highest usage of its services between 2021 and 2025, according to Health Department data. Lauderdale, Alcorn, George, Jones and Forrest counties all served over 100 mothers and infants during the five-year period.
The Mississippi counties with the highest infant mortality rates from 2015 to 2024, which include Quitman, Attala, Washington, Claiborne and Holmes counties, were not selected for the program.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bill creating long-term care insurance safeguards in CT wins final passage
description: The bill requires insurers to file annual reports with the state on incurred and actual paid losses for long-term care insurance policies.
text:
Legislation that creates safeguards for long-term care insurance policyholders and requires greater financial disclosures from carriers won final passage in the Connecticut House late Tuesday, marking a significant step toward adding transparency to the industry.
The measure cleared the chamber with broad bipartisan support after just three minutes of discussion. Members voted 146-4 in favor.
The bill requires insurers to file annual reports with the state on incurred and actual paid losses for long-term care insurance policies issued in Connecticut. The state insurance commissioner and head of the governor’s budget office must share the information with legislators and post it on their departments’ websites.
It also gives the state attorney general the power to investigate insurance companies for practices or patterns that violate state law.
Additionally, the measure directs the insurance commissioner to study the effects of a proposal allowing policyholders to cancel their plans — and obtain full refunds for premiums paid since the start of the coverage — whenever an insurer files for rate hikes that exceed the rate of inflation. It also asks the commissioner to review the impact of the reinsurance market on the availability of long-term care insurance policies.
“We made a major step in the right direction,” said Jan Kritzman, 78, after watching the bill sail through the House. Kritzman’s long-term care coverage with her husband has risen to $7,000 a year, up from $2,000 when they purchased the plans in 2004.
“We just we want accountability. We want an answer to, ‘Why are you raising the rates?’ We will certainly keep an eye on how the Connecticut Insurance Department goes forth with this. Hopefully they will be on the side of the policyholders who are in dire need of help from oppressive, burdensome rate increases.”
Nearly 100,000 people in Connecticut have long-term care insurance — coverage that, depending on the policy, supports skilled in-home care, rehabilitation therapy, assisted living, nursing home stays and respite care.
A Connecticut Mirror investigation last year found that the annual cost of maintaining long-term care coverage has risen sharply for many residents due to miscalculations by insurers on how long people would live, the price of care and how many would need it. Policyholders complained of dramatic rate increases, often exceeding 50% and, for a few dozen people, as high as 174%, according to a CT Mirror analysis.
The CT Mirror’s review of rate hikes from January 2019 to October 2024 showed that more than 17,000 people with long-term care policies were had been hit with increases of 50% or more. Some of the biggest companies in the market, including Genworth Financial, Metropolitan Life Insurance Company and Transamerica Life Insurance Company, requested hikes for five years in a row beginning in 2019.
[Read all of CT Mirror’s coverage of the long-term care insurance industry here.]
When large providers seek premium increases, thousands of consumers can be affected. In 2019, for example, Genworth Financial requested a 40% rate hike on more than 9,000 Connecticut policyholders. In 2021, Transamerica requested a 20% rate increase on 8,000 policies. The insurance department approved both requests with no changes.
In 2022, Genworth raised rates for more than 2,000 people by an average of 97%, with increases ranging from 79% to 173%, depending on the policy. The approved amounts were a slight reduction from the company’s original request.
The long-term care insurance bill passed the Senate last week.
“This is a step forward that will hopefully provide some compensation, some sign to the people of this state that we care about this issue, that we are aware the market has failed the people who purchased these policies,” Sen. Matthew Lesser, D-Middletown, a key back of the measure, said during the debate.
The legislation now heads to Gov. Ned Lamont’s desk.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: After ousting his critics, Landry appointee seeks more control over Louisiana public defenders
description: Gov. Jeff Landry’s appointee who runs Louisiana’s public defender system is seeking more control over its remaining attorneys and budget, having already eliminated five of his most vocal critics from the network.
text:
Rémy Starns, Louisiana's state public defender, is seeking more control over the public defender system's remaining attorneys and budget, having already eliminated five of his most vocal critics. Gov. Jeff Landry’s appointee who runs Louisiana’s public defender system is seeking more control over its remaining attorneys and budget, having already eliminated five of his most vocal critics. 
Rémy Starns, the state’s public defender, oversees the government-funded legal counsel criminal defendants receive when they cannot afford to pay for their own defense. The public defender system provided attorneys to approximately 140,000 people in 2025, or almost 88% of all criminal defendants in Louisiana, according to the system’s annual report.  
Starns asked state lawmakers this year to guarantee his agency will get tens of millions of dollars annually that can’t be cut. At the same time, he wants the Louisiana Legislature to weaken the ability of a state Public Defender Oversight Board and judges to overturn his financial decisions. 
The proposals Starns backs this year are in three pieces of legislation: House Bill 1005, by Rep. Nicholas Muscarello, R-Hammond; Senate Bill 316, by Sen. Mike Reese, R-Leesville; and Senate Bill 448 by Sen. Jay Luneau, D-Alexandria. 
His requests come after lawmakers granted the state public defender, and by extension the governor, more control over the wider public defender system and its budget two years ago. 
That shift of power led to several months of turmoil in public defender management, during which over half of the Public Defender Oversight Board quit. Starns also forced five attorneys running local public defender offices out of their jobs after they criticized his policies publicly. 
Four of the dismissed lawyers are now suing him and his state agency for alleged wrongful termination. 
A few of the law changes Starns seeks this spring mirror those legislators have rejected from him over the past two years. But public opposition was more fierce previously. 
In 2024, about 20 of the state’s 37 chief public defenders who run local offices showed up to legislative committee meetings to testify against bills Starns was pushing. Last year, five local chief defenders — all who had received notice they were losing their jobs – appeared at a legislative hearing to push back on Starns legislation. 
Last month, just one former public defender, who Starns ousted last year, came to oppose the Muscarello bill at a Louisiana House committee hearing. 

“The other 37 chiefs are afraid that if they speak up, that they’ll be fired,” said Brett Brunson, who had been chief public defender in Natchitoches Parish for 18 years before losing his position. 

At legislative hearings, Starns has said the public defense system has been on more stable financial footing since he took more control over the network. 

“The reforms of 2024 are working. Our system has never been better than it is today,” he told the Senate Finance Committee last week.

But Starns declined to answer additional questions about the legislation he is backing. 

“You know I’m not going to answer any of your questions,” he told a reporter who approached him for an interview last week.

Jeffrey Hufft, a Metairie attorney who Landry appointed chair of the Public Defender Oversight Board last year, did not return phone calls and texts seeking comment for this report.  
 Board would lose say over hiring state public defender

Muscarello’s proposal would make two substantive changes for Starns that lawmakers have been unwilling to support previously. 
The bill would eliminate a requirement for a Public Defender Oversight Board vote to confirm the state public defender to a new term every two years. It would continue the Louisiana Senate confirmation requirement for the gubernatorial appointee. 
This change would eliminate any say the Louisiana Supreme Court, Louisiana House Speaker, Louisiana Association of Criminal Defense Attorneys and Public Defenders Association of Louisiana have in vetting the nominee. Under current law, all of those entities — plus the governor and state Senate president — help pick oversight board members. 

Critics said Starns’ proposed restructuring creates governance problems and runs afoul of American Bar Association guidance because it consolidates too much power over public defense under the governor. 

The state, run by the governor, is responsible for bringing criminal charges against all defendants, including those facing the death penalty. There is a concern that the governor having too much direct control over the defendants’ attorneys, including in death penalty cases, could interfere with their ability to get proper legal representation. 
“[The bill] takes all of the independence away and all of the insight from any other branch of government away,” said Jim Boren, a Baton Rouge criminal defense attorney and former state public defender board member, of the legislation.

The timing of the law change would occur right as Starns faces confirmation again. He was initially selected to be the state public defender by former Gov. John Bel Edwards in 2020 and reappointed to the job by Landry in 2024. 

The Muscarello legislation would also transfer control over the compensation of the chief public defenders who run local district offices from the board to the state public defender. District defender compensation has been an ongoing dispute between Starns and board members.  

In 2024, a new board made up mostly of Landry appointees voted twice to reject Starns’ pay scale for these jobs. The members were uncomfortable that Starns’ plan would result in some public defender chiefs losing tens of thousands of dollars in pay annually. 

The House has voted 71-19 for the Muscarello bill, which is now in the Senate for consideration. 
 Expert witness funding

Under Senate Bill 448, by Luneau, the state public defender’s office would no longer provide funding for expert witnesses to indigent defendants represented by private attorneys instead of a public defender. 
Private lawyers sometimes volunteer to represent poor defendants for free and judges also occasionally direct private attorneys to handle cases for overburdened public defenders at no cost. 
“One of the problems that we have is courts will order the public defenders’ office to pay for expert witness funds for people we don’t represent,” Starns said at a Senate judiciary committee meeting on the bill last month. 

The legislation essentially shores up a more sweeping state law that says judges cannot force the state public defender or public defender district offices to pay for any oservice on behalf of a defendant. 

But the Louisiana Supreme Court ruled Friday that the law in question is unconstitutional. because it impedes on the judicial branch of government and could obstruct a defendants’ rights to fair legal representation. 

The ruling stemmed from the case of Maya Jones, who has been charged alongside her boyfriend with killing her 2-year-old son, Ezekiel Harry. Jones initially faced the death penalty, though prosecutors have since abandoned that plan. 
Starns had denied Jones’ legal team, which includes private attorneys, funding to hire community polling experts. But a district court judge overturned Starns’ decision, ordering the state public defender to provide the funding for the expert. The Supreme Court backed the lower court’s decision. 
Rick Schroeder, a private attorney representing Jones pro bono, said Luneau’s legislation would make it very difficult for private attorneys to represent indigent defendants pro bono. The attorney can provide their own services at no cost but often can’t afford to hire experts out of pocket without help from the state, he said. 
“It’s part of the overall attempt to have control over everything related to public defense,” said Schroeder, who also represents the former chief district defenders in their lawsuit against Starns over losing their jobs. 

The Senate voted 36-0 in favor of the Luneau legislation, which is now in the House for consideration. 
 A request for guaranteed money

Senate Bill 316, by Reese, would tie state funding for public defense each year to the amount of money district attorneys receive. It would essentially create a financial floor of $47.1 million for public defender services statewide and ensure the system’s funding increases every time district attorney state funding goes up, starting in the 2027-28 fiscal year. 

“If there are more people in court prosecuting, there needs to be more people in court defending,” Starns told the Senate Finance Committee last week. 
The proposal has stalled over senators’ concerns about losing lawmaker control over the public defense funding level, particularly when only the state public defender would oversee the spending. 

“If the legislature disagrees with whoever person is in that position and, you know, they’re guaranteed a certain amount of money, I mean the legislature can’t remove that person,” Sen. Thomas Pressly, R-Shreveport said. 

Starns responded by saying the old state public defender board, which had more authority over his office’s spending before 2024, had “wrecked everything” by making poor spending decisions. 

“I’m appointed by the governor and subject to Senate confirmation, which is a significant check. I don’t see why there’s a need for anything more significant than that,” he told the senators.

name: Michigan Advance
title: McDonald Rivet speaks to Saginaw parents about childcare costs, highlights tax credit bill
description: U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) hosted a roundtable discussion with three Saginaw parents on Wednesday morning, emphasizing the high costs of childcare and the need for relief for working parents — including through a tax credit proposal that she has introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives. “What my proposal would do is give […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) plays with children at Jerome Preschool in Saginaw following a roundtable with parents about childcare costs. May 6, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) hosted a roundtable discussion with three Saginaw parents on Wednesday morning, emphasizing the high costs of childcare and the need for relief for working parents — including through a tax credit proposal that she has introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives.
“What my proposal would do is give a tax credit to families with incomes of $100,000 or less, $5,500 for every child age 3 and under each year to help pay for those expenses,” she explained.
All three parents agreed that having that amount of money would be a relief, with Toria Williams, who has one young son, saying that it would take a “weight off.”
Saginaw parents speak about their childcare costs with U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City). May 6, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Marcos Ponce, who has five children, added that it would allow him and his family to put away money for savings and investments.
Williams, whose son attends a specialized preschool in the Saginaw Independent School District, said that childcare would cost her around $600 per week if he were not enrolled in the school program. 
Meanwhile, Kaycee Cook, the mom of seven children, said that after giving birth to twin daughters, it was more cost-efficient for her to become a stay-at-home mom than to pay for childcare for both girls.
Cook noted that diapers and food are the biggest costs to her family, spending at least $40 per week on diapers alone, which “adds up really quickly” when she currently has three children in diapers.
Ponce and Williams added that, on top of childcare costs, rising cost of living — including utility bills and rent — has made it harder for them to give their children what they want and need.
U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) hosted a roundtable in Saginaw to discuss childcare costs and her bill to create a tax cut for working parents of children under three. May 6, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
McDonald Rivet’s bill, introduced in mid-April, would establish a similar system to Michigan’s Working Families Tax Credit, which she worked on while in the state Senate. 
“It’s about where our tax dollars go and how much of families’ incomes go to paying their taxes,” she said. “This is about a tax credit, which you have to work in order to qualify for.”
She also told reporters after the event that she is beginning to see bipartisan support for the legislation. 
“I think that everyone can recognize how expensive the first three years of parenting can be. Everybody recognizes that the cost of child care is skyrocketing in a way that most families can’t afford it,” she said. “If we’re going to give somebody a tax cut, it needs to be families like the ones we just talked to who are working really, really hard, but paying for the expenses of an infant and a toddler just seem out of reach for them.”

title: Attorney Whitney Lipscomb is running for secretary of state
description: Whitney Lipscomb
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Whitney Lipscomb, an attorney who has worked for Republican officials in Mississippi, will run for secretary of state next year, according to campaign finance forms. 
Lipscomb’s campaign committee filed its initial paperwork recently with the secretary of state’s office saying she plans to run. 
“I’m grateful for the encouragement I’ve received across Mississippi,” Lipscomb said in a statement. “People want strong, conservative leaders who will stand with President Trump, protect election integrity, and fight hard to defend our values and way of life. I am taking the necessary steps, spending time in prayer and listening as I chart a path forward. Stay tuned!” 
Lipscomb was deputy chief of staff and an attorney for former Gov. Phil Bryant and served as deputy attorney general under AG Lynn Fitch. She left Fitch’s office last year and became the general counsel for the Republican Attorneys General Association. 
It’s expected that Lipscomb will launch her campaign for secretary of state in the coming weeks. 
Shuwaski Young, the Democratic nominee for secretary of state in 2023, previously announced that he is running again for the position next year as a Republican. No Democratic candidate has announced a run for the office. 
Current Secretary of State Michael Watson is running for lieutenant governor next year. The secretary of state’s office is responsible for training local election officials, helping administer elections and handling business registration.
