name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Q&A: Iowa GOP gubernatorial candidates on abortion, eminent domain, ESAs
description: It wasn’t a debate, but all five Republicans running for Iowa’s open gubernatorial seat recently answered a set of questions on abortion, eminent domain, public funding for private schools through the state’s Educational Savings Account (ESA) program and more. The interviews took place in front of more than 1,000 people at the Horizon Events Center […]
text:
Former state representative and pastor Brad Sherman, left, talks with Republican Party of Iowa Chairman Jeff Kaufmann May 1, 2026 at the at the Iowa Faith and Freedom Coalition's Spring Kickoff event in Clive. (Photo by Kadin Luhmann for Iowa Capital Dispatch)It wasn’t a debate, but all five Republicans running for Iowa’s open gubernatorial seat recently answered a set of questions on abortion, eminent domain, public funding for private schools through the state’s Educational Savings Account (ESA) program and more.
The interviews took place in front of more than 1,000 people at the Horizon Events Center in Clive on May 1 as part of the Iowa Faith and Freedom Coalition’s (IFFC) 26th annual Spring Kickoff event. 
IFFC is a nonprofit activist organization that promotes conservatism and evangelicalism.
State Rep. Eddie Andrews, U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, farmer and businessman Zach Lahn, former state representative and pastor Brad Sherman and former Iowa Department of Administrative Services director Adam Steen answered questions from Republican Party of Iowa Chairman Jeff Kaufmann.
Feenstra, in particular, has been criticized for skipping forums and debates involving the other candidates. Last week’s “Iowa Press” debate only included three of the five candidates, with Lahn also absent.
 The candidates were asked the same five questions and their responses are summarized below.
Q: What does being pro-life mean to you?
Steen: Life at conception is “foundational” and “fundamental,” he said.
Iowa Republican gubernatorial candidate Adam Steen participates in a debate hosted by Iowa PBS on April 28, 2026, in Johnston, Iowa.
Steen added that he supports measures to restrict abortion medications from being sent to Iowans through mail. The Iowa Senate passed House File 2563 on Sunday, which restricts access to abortion-inducing medication through telehealth and mail-order prescription services.
“Those abortion pills that are being sent to the state of Iowa right now, we have to stop those,” Steen said. “Get those out of here and ensure that life is protected.”
Sherman: He said he would like to expand Iowa’s 2023 “heartbeat” bill, House File 732, that restricts abortions in Iowa when a fetal heartbeat is detectable.
“I don’t think you can be more pro-life than I am,” Sherman said. “I was happy to vote for the heartbeat bill when I was in the Legislature, but we need to go all the way to life at conception.”
Lahn: He said he is unapologetically pro-life at conception. Lahn added that protection of life does not end at birth, and advocated for healthier food, less medication for children and clean water. 
“I’m very proud to be the first candidate ever to be endorsed by the Make America Healthy Again organization that is fighting for Bobby Kennedy’s principles in D.C.,” Lahn said. “The next generation is facing a reality that they’re the first generation in recorded history to likely have a lower lifespan than previous generations.”
Andrews: He co-sponsored a proposed life at conception bill in the Iowa House, he said.
“I just signed on to a life at conception bill, so I think everyone knows I don’t just talk the talk, I walk the walk,” Andrews said. “There’s a reason why ‘Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness’ is a phrase we always use. It starts with life, and we need to 100% protect it.”
Feenstra: He proudly voted for President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” that prohibited, for one year, the use of Medicaid for Planned Parenthood services, he said.
“We’ve got to take care of women, work with them, walk beside them and tell them how important their child is,” Feenstra said.
Q: How will you protect religious freedom?
Feenstra: It is important to promote Christianity, he said.
“We have to make sure that everyone knows what we stand for as Christians,” Feenstra said. “We have a right to religious liberty.”
Andrews: During his time in the Legislature, religious liberty in Iowa has been strengthened, he said.
“I’m the only guy here who has actually voted for religious freedom,” Andrews said. “The First Amendment is first for a reason. It’s designed to protect your right to have religious expression and freedom of speech. It goes to the individual’s right to express worship in the way you see fit without any risk of government intervention.”
Sherman: His campaign slogan, “Restoring the Foundations of Freedom,” came from his desire to teach and share his worldview of putting religious principles in the public eye, he said.
“I’ve been a pastor for 45 years, and we’ve been fighting this battle to put godly principles back into the public square for decades,” Sherman said. “This is my heartbeat to restore the foundations of freedom, and wokeism is trying to destroy that.”
Lahn: Left-wing politicians have attacked religious liberties by promoting political ideology and “wokeism” in public schools, he said.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn spoke with supporters who came to celebrate the opening of his West Des Moines campaign headquarters April 2, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“Wokeism, I believe, is a mental disorder,” Lahn said. “It absolutely is. It is one that is aimed at destroying the foundations of our society and making us easier to control.”
Steen: He shared a story about how he and his wife prevented “Jacob’s New Dress,” a fictional book about a boy who enjoys wearing dresses, from being read in his son’s preschool class.
“We have to keep that woke, radical ideology out of our schools, out of our churches, out of everywhere,” Steen said. “We need to ensure that our families, our children, first and foremost, are protected. Otherwise, we’ve got nothing left.”
Q: What are your views on eminent domain?
Andrews: He said he was part of a group that coined the phrase, “No eminent domain for private gain” several years ago.
“The government’s job is to protect your rights,” Andrews said. “I will be the strongest pro-property governor that we have ever had.”
Steen: Iowa lawmakers need to make property rights and the prevention of eminent domain abuse a priority, specifically for carbon sequestration, he said.
“We have to solve that issue this legislative session,” Steen said. “This is a critical issue. I will protect your property rights.”
Despite eminent domain being a prominent issue for Iowa Republican lawmakers, no legislation was passed during the 2026 session to address the concerns.
Feenstra:  Agriculture is Iowa’s economic engine, he said, and eminent domain abuse puts the state’s family farms and other property owners at risk.
U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra appears on Iowa PBS’ “Iowa Press” show on Dec. 18, 2020. (Screenshot from Iowa PBS)
“Property belongs to the American farmer,” Feenstra said. “If somebody wants to run a pipeline, or whatever it might be, then it’s negotiated between the private property owner and the business, and if the private property owner says, ‘No,’ that’s it.”
Sherman: Property rights are a foundational principle for freedom in the U.S, he said, and warned against the abuse of eminent domain.
“A private company who is not a common carrier for a product that’s not a public utility should never get to use the domain,” Sherman said.
Lahn: “I’m very happy that the other candidates support this the way I do,” Lahn said. “No eminent domain for private gain here.”
He added that one of the reasons people migrated to the U.S. during the nation’s infancy was for the opportunity to own property, describing the right to own property as “foundational.”
“They didn’t have the ability to own the ground under their feet,” Lahn said. I’ve fought this on my own property and I’ve won.”
Q: What is your view of “school choice?”
Steen: The ESA program is one of the “greatest pieces of legislation” the state has passed in recent years. 
Steen said public school educators face “ridiculous” standards that restrict their ability to teach, sharing that his 10-year-old son is graded on how fast he can read.
“He reads with 100% accuracy and 100% fluency, but he has a rare genetic disorder that doesn’t allow him to read fast,” Steen said. “We get zeroes on his papers, and with tears in their eyes, teachers will look at us and say, ‘This is what we are required to grade him by.’”
Steen said his proposal to strengthen Iowa public schools would involve implementing a classical education approach, an educational philosophy that emphasizes critical thinking.
Feenstra: Education in Iowa should be “robust,” and parents should have full control over their child’s education.
“I’m a product of school choice and my children are products of school choice,” Feenstra said. “We both went to Christian schools. If a parent wants to send their kids to a charter school, a Christian school, wherever that might be, they should be able to have that choice.”
Feenstra has faced criticism from Republicans, including Steen, for saying he would consider requirements for private schools that accept public funds through the ESA program to accept all students, as public schools must.
Lahn: He said he would expand the ESA program, as well as working to improve the quality of public schools.
“The governor of Iowa must be the number one advocate for public school kids in the state,” Lahn said. “I can’t wait to get in and work on the culture and quality of our public schools, so private schools also have to compete with them. It makes everybody better.”
Andrews: He said he has voted for various  measures to expand the ESA program.
Iowa Rep. Eddie Andrews, a Republican gubernatorial candidate, spoke to reporters as he and his attorney responded to a challenge to his campaign’s nomination papers before the State Objection Panel hearing March 24, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“I led the push for regular district school choice, district-to-district school choice and then public charter school choice,” Andrews said. “All parents have the right to educate their child in the way that is best for that child.”
Sherman: He said he voted for the ESA program and supports parents having control over their child’s education.
Sherman added that he “appreciates” public schools, saying he wants to reform public education by implementing specific principles.
“We need to replace common core with common sense,” Sherman said. “We need to put constitutional values of principles and patriotism, etc. back into our children’s minds at the elementary level.”
Q: What do you want people to know about your campaign?
Steen: He said he is guided by a biblical worldview, and his government and business experience will be an advantage in a head-to-head matchup with Democratic candidate Rob Sand.
“Rob Sand is doing everything he can to come in and decimate this state,” Steen said. “Adam Steen, the candidate, not only has the business background, not only has the government operations background, but he’s got the worldview, the tenacity and the ability to take on Rob Sand.”
Iowa Republican gubernatorial candidate Brad Sherman participates in a debate hosted by Iowa PBS on April 28, 2026, in Johnston, Iowa.
Sherman: He said he has literal “swamp draining” experience, highlighting his past farm work, and advocated for more transparency in government programs.
“A big priority for me is to initiate programs to bring transparency into our government,” Sherman said.
Feenstra: He wants Iowa to be the most business and agriculture-friendly state in the U.S., he said, while emphasizing affordable healthcare and the protection of the First and Second Amendments of the Constitution.
“We stand on the Bible and we stand on the Constitution and that’s how I’ll govern,” Feenstra said. “Together, we will beat Rob Sand.”
Lahn: His campaign is focused on four main issues: keeping children in the state, preventing eminent domain abuse, making Iowa’s education the best in the U.S. and addressing the state’s high cancer rates, he said.
“Our campaign is about putting Iowa first,” Lahn said. “We have great momentum in this race. We are here to win on June 2.”
Andrews: He has won three consecutive elections in a “purple” district and can appeal to moderate voters, he said. He added that he is influenced by the approach that Ronald Reagan and Charlie Kirk took to politics.
 “I have singlehandedly added more Republican votes than any other district in Iowa,” Andrews said. “We’re going to want a person who can address just like Ronald Reagan, hold that banner high and attract people that are not just Republicans, but also people that are in the middle, and I’m the only one with the receipts.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Democrat Jennifer Jenkins now says she’ll run for CD 8 seat in Brevard County
description: Former Brevard County Democratic school board member Jennifer Jenkins, at one time a candidate for U.S. Senate, is dropping her bid against Republican Randy Fine in Florida’s Sixth Congressional District and will run instead in Florida’s Eight District, now held by Republican Mike Haridopolos. Several Democratic and Republican challengers are expected to swi[...]
text:
Former Brevard County School Board member Jennifer Jenkins speaking in Centennial Park in Ybor City in Tampa on May 7, 2023. (Credit: Mitch Perry)Former Brevard County Democratic school board member Jennifer Jenkins, at one time a candidate for U.S. Senate, is dropping her bid against Republican Randy Fine in Florida’s Sixth Congressional District and will run instead in Florida’s Eight District, now held by Republican Mike Haridopolos.
Several Democratic and Republican challengers are expected to switch their races for Congress now that the congressional map has been significantly altered by Gov. Ron DeSantis and the Legislature.
That map keeps Brevard County whole while adding a portion of eastern Orange County, incorporating the University of Central Florida and surrounding areas.
“Once the Legislature passed these maps, I received several calls from around Brevard and Orange counties asking me to run here,” Jenkins said Tuesday in a written statement. “District 8 voters have pain at the pump, a struggle to afford adequate health care, and a representative who dodges town halls and real conversations with the people he’s supposed to serve.”
Haridopolos served in the Legislature from 2000 through 2012, including his last two years as Senate president. He was elected to serve in CD 8 in 2024, jumping into the race on the last day of qualifying, on the same day then-GOP incumbent Bill Posey announced his retirement from Congress.
The Republican Party of Florida in a statement noted that Jenkins has now twice switched races this year.
“Jennifer ‘Jumpin’ Jenkins keep jumping — race to race, district to district — chasing whatever might stick,” said RPOF Chairman Evan Power. “Floridians want a leader who fights for them and their community, not someone shopping for a seat.”
Jenkins’ chances of election this year may have improved with her switch. Fine won the CD 6 seat over Democrat Josh Weil in a special election last year by 14 points. That margin was more than half of what took place in 2024, when then-GOP-incumbent Mike Waltz won the seat by 30 points.
Haridopolos’ CD 8 seat, on the other hand, is a little less Republican-leaning than it was before the new map was approved last week. Donald Trump won it by more than 22 points in 2024 but, according to data analyst Matt Isbell, CD 8 is now a +16.1% Trump seat.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Senate president welcomes praise for 2026 Legislature’s work on Trump agenda
description: Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson, who is a GOP candidate for governor, hails White House letter of appreciation for work of 2026 Legislature.
text:
Senate President Ty Masterson, right, and House Speaker Dan Hawkins received a letter from the White House Office of Intergovernmental Affairs praising the 2026 Kansas Legislature's support of priorities set forth by President Donald Trump. This is a 2025 image Masterson and Hawkins chatting at the Kansas Capitol. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson publicly shared a letter signed by a White House staff member praising the GOP-led Kansas Legislature for tackling issues of wasteful government spending and broadening financial support of private education.
The letter addressed to Masterson, the Andover president of the Kansas Senate, and Kansas House Speaker Dan Hawkins of Wichita, congratulated state legislators for working during the 2026 session to advance elements of President Donald Trump’s agenda. Masterson is among the Republican field of candidates for governor, while Hawkins is seeking election as state insurance commissioner.
“We applaud your dedication to deliver on President Trump’s priorities and your leadership and courage … in enacting many priorities via veto override,” said Alex Meyer, director of the White House Office of Intergovernmental Affairs.
On Monday, Masterson said he was proud of Senate support for the Trump administration and of politically positioning Kansas as a conservative model for other states.
“From day one, our mission was clear: Advance President Trump’s America First agenda right here in Kansas,” Masterson said. “We didn’t just talk about it. We delivered.”
Masterson pointed to actions of the Legislature to reduce wasteful spending, strengthen election integrity, expand resources for private schools and protect first responders.
In terms of state spending, the Legislature placed into law a requirement state agencies enter data-matching agreements to verify eligibility for government food and medical assistance. State lawmakers moved to prohibit Kansans from self-reporting income level or household size when applying for assistance.
Democrats in the House and Senate opposed the legislation because it would deny food aid to thousands of Kansans. Gov. Laura Kelly vetoed the bill, but the Legislature overrode the Democratic governor.
The Legislature eliminated “no-excuse” absentee voting and restricted what online websites could be used to register voters. State agencies involved in registration were ordered to share personal data, such as a Social Security numbers, with the Kansas secretary of state’s office.
Opponents of data-sharing questioned the legality of the mandate and warned that computer searches would result in accidental flagging of U.S. citizens who had a right to vote.
The Legislature overrode Kelly’s veto of a bill establishing a 25-foot buffer zone around law enforcement and emergency personnel. Individuals who intentionally remained in the zone could be charged with a misdemeanor and possibly sentenced to six months in jail. Kansas also granted county sheriffs authority to enter agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement without approval of county commissions.
Supporters of the changes said it was to protect first responders from interference by protesters who objected to federal immigration actions. Kelly vetoed the bill, citing First Amendment considerations, but the veto was overridden.
“This legislation creates serious tension between ensuring law enforcement officers can carry out their duties while respecting the First Amendment rights of Kansans to observe and record their actions,” Kelly said.
The Legislature deflected Kelly’s veto of a bill enabling Kansas to take part in the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit program. It offers a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit up to $1,700 starting in 2027 for donations to organizations awarding scholarships to students attending private schools in Kansas.
“This new federal program needs to be thoroughly vetted to understand the potential impact on funding for our public schools,” Kelly said. “If it is, in essence, just another voucher program designed to redirect taxpayer dollars to private schools to the detriment of our public schools, Kansans have made clear they don’t want it.”
The House and Senate also expanded to $20 million the annual cap on state tax credits issued to support scholarships for lower-income students at private schools.

name: Delaware
title: Los latinos impulsan la economía cambiante de Delaware
description: A medida que crece la población latina en Delaware, también aumenta su influencia en la fuerza laboral, los pequeños negocios y el futuro económico del estado. En cualquier mañana en Delaware, los trabajadores latinos ya están ayudando a dar forma al día: vertiendo concreto en obras de construcción, preparando comidas en restaurantes familiares, manteniendo[...]
text:
A medida que crece la población latina en Delaware, también aumenta su influencia en la fuerza laboral, los pequeños negocios y el futuro económico del estado.
En cualquier mañana en Delaware, los trabajadores latinos ya están ayudando a dar forma al día: vertiendo concreto en obras de construcción, preparando comidas en restaurantes familiares, manteniendo hogares y negocios, y apoyando los servicios de los que dependen las comunidades.
Lo que puede parecer trabajo cotidiano forma parte de una historia mucho más grande: una de las comunidades de más rápido crecimiento en el estado también se está convirtiendo en uno de sus motores económicos más importantes.
Delaware tiene poco más de 1 millón de habitantes, y los latinos representan más del 10% de la población, según estimaciones del Censo de EE. UU. Esa proporción tendrá implicaciones a largo plazo para las escuelas, la fuerza laboral y la comunidad empresarial del estado.
El impacto va más allá del crecimiento poblacional.
Los inmigrantes en Delaware contribuyen con aproximadamente 1.4 mil millones de dólares en impuestos y cuentan con 4.2 mil millones de dólares en poder de compra, según el American Immigration Council. Ese dinero circula a través de negocios locales, vivienda, servicios de alimentos y la actividad económica diaria.
El emprendimiento latino también está creciendo en todo el estado. Muchos negocios comienzan siendo pequeños, construidos con esfuerzo familiar, confianza y recomendaciones de boca en boca, pero desempeñan un papel clave en sus comunidades.
Desde restaurantes y servicios de limpieza hasta jardinería y construcción, los negocios propiedad de latinos están generando ingresos, empleos y oportunidades.
“No se trata de venir a este país esperando recibir, sino también de aportar”, dijo Emmanuel Huerta, un empresario mexicano en Delaware.
Ese sentido de responsabilidad y contribución impulsa a muchos negocios latinos en todo el estado.
A medida que Delaware continúa evolucionando, se espera que las comunidades latinas desempeñen un papel aún mayor en la configuración de su futuro. Sus contribuciones ya no son emergentes. Son esenciales.
Desde pequeños negocios hasta grandes industrias, los latinos no solo participan en la economía de Delaware. Están ayudando a construirla.
Notas del Editor
Los latinos representan más del 10% de la población de Delaware y constituyen uno de los grupos demográficos de más rápido crecimiento en el estado.
Los inmigrantes en Delaware contribuyen aproximadamente 1.4 mil millones de dólares en impuestos y cuentan con cerca de 4.2 mil millones de dólares en poder adquisitivo, lo que respalda a los negocios y la actividad económica local.
El crecimiento de los trabajadores y empresarios latinos seguirá desempeñando un papel clave en la futura fuerza laboral y economía de Delaware.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear says he’s signing emergency measures to freeze, lower gas tax
description: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is signing emergency measures to freeze the state’s sales tax on gasoline starting in July and declare a state of emergency that could potentially lower the tax by 10 cents a gallon starting next week.  In a Tuesday press conference, Beshear, said he doesn’t see an end to the ongoing war […]
text:
Gov. Andy Beshear will sign an emergency order to lower gas prices. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is signing emergency measures to freeze the state’s sales tax on gasoline starting in July and declare a state of emergency that could potentially lower the tax by 10 cents a gallon starting next week. 
In a Tuesday press conference, Beshear, said he doesn’t see an end to the ongoing war between Iran and the United States that’s contributing to surging gasoline and diesel prices, arguing the measures would cumulatively save Kentuckians tens of millions of dollars at the gas pump each month. 
“Our families are feeling the pain. They’re being forced to make tough decisions, decisions like choosing between food and medication, the money just isn’t stretching through the month,” Beshear said. “The price of gas isn’t partisan. It’s not Democrat or Republican. It’s just too high.” 
The average price of regular gasoline and diesel in Kentucky is at $4.28 and $5.32, respectively, as of Tuesday, according to AAA. Gasoline prices across the country have spiked since the outbreak of the war with Iran; the Energy Information Administration states regular gasoline prices across the country are, on average, more than a $1.30 higher compared to last year. 
Beshear, a Democrat, said Republican Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman would have to sign off on the state of emergency that would lower the state’s gas tax by 10 cents a gallon starting May 11. 
“My hope is the AG sees it the same way that I do, that saving families 10 cents a gallon at the pump right now is the right thing to do,” Beshear said.
When asked by a reporter if he believes Republicans in the GOP-controlled state legislature would support the emergency moves, Beshear pointed to a move by Republican Indiana Gov. Mike Braun to suspend the sales tax on gas. 
Requests for comment to spokespeople for GOP leadership in the legislature and for Coleman did not immediately return requests for comment.
This story will be updated.

name: Delaware
title: Latinos help power Delaware’s changing economy by Yoselin Negrete
description: On Cinco De Mayo:  Delaware’s Latino population grows & so does its influence on the state’s workforce, small businesses and future economy. By Yoselin Negrete, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE WILMINGTON, DE – On any given morning in Delaware, Latino workers are already helping shape the day — pouring concrete on construction sites, preparing meals in[...]
text:
On Cinco De Mayo:  Delaware’s Latino population grows & so does its influence on the state’s workforce, small businesses and future economy.

By Yoselin Negrete, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE

WILMINGTON, DE – On any given morning in Delaware, Latino workers are already helping shape the day — pouring concrete on construction sites, preparing meals in family-owned restaurants, maintaining homes and businesses, and supporting the services communities rely on.
What may look like everyday work is part of a much larger story: one of the state’s fastest-growing communities is also one of its increasingly important economic drivers.
Delaware is home to just over 1 million residents, and Latinos make up more than 10% of the population, according to U.S. Census estimates. That share is expected to carry long-term implications for Delaware’s schools, workforce and business community.
The impact goes beyond population growth.
Immigrants in Delaware contribute an estimated $1.4 billion in taxes and hold $4.2 billion in spending power, according to the American Immigration Council. That money moves through local businesses, housing, food services and everyday economic activity.
Latino entrepreneurship is also growing across the state. Many businesses start small, built on family effort, trust and word-of-mouth, but they play a major role in local communities.
From restaurants and cleaning services to landscaping and contracting, Latino-owned businesses are creating income, jobs and opportunity.
“No se trata de venir a este país esperando recibir, sino también de aportar,” said Emmanuel Huerta, a Mexican entrepreneur in Delaware.
“It’s not just about coming to this country expecting to receive — but also about contributing.”
As Delaware continues to change, Latino communities are expected to play an even greater role in shaping its future. Their contributions are no longer emerging. They are essential.
From small businesses to major industries, Latinos are not just participating in Delaware’s economy. They are helping build it.
Editor’s Notes
Latinos represent more than 10% of Delaware’s population and are among the state’s fastest-growing demographic groups.
Immigrants in Delaware contribute an estimated $1.4 billion in taxes and hold approximately $4.2 billion in spending power, supporting businesses and local economic activity.
The growth of Latino workers and entrepreneurs is expected to play a significant role in shaping Delaware’s future workforce and economy.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas legislators advance tax cuts; last round of votes expected Wednesday
description: Democrats’ warnings about looming federal funding cuts and unmet needs didn’t dissuade the predominantly-Republican Arkansas House and Senate Tuesday from overwhelmingly advancing income tax cuts. Lawmakers on Wednesday are expected to give final approval to separate but identical bills outlining the cuts proposed by Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders. T[...]
text:
Rep. Stephen Magie (center left, standing) speaks with Rep. Mark McElroy (center right, standing) before House votes get underway on May 5, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Democrats’ warnings about looming federal funding cuts and unmet needs didn’t dissuade the predominantly-Republican Arkansas House and Senate Tuesday from overwhelmingly advancing income tax cuts.
Lawmakers on Wednesday are expected to give final approval to separate but identical bills outlining the cuts proposed by Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders. The governor called a special session that began Monday focused solely on the cuts.
The legislation calls for cutting taxes on personal income over $26,400 to 3.7%, retroactive to Jan. 1 of this year, while reducing the corporate income tax to 4.1% starting next year. The current individual and corporate tax rates are 3.9% and 4.3%, respectively.
The cuts faced criticism from Democrats who said the reductions in revenue as well as the budget surplus Arkansas is accumulating come at the expense of other needs in the state.
“If I’ve got a thousand bucks, and after my most critical expenses I’m lucky enough to have $100 left, but I know I’ve got a cavity and bald tires on my car, I do not have a surplus,” Democratic Sen. Greg Leding of Fayetteville told the Senate. “I’m just choosing to ignore some very obvious problems.”
The legislation passed on party-line votes in both chambers, with it passing the Senate 29-6 and the House 79-17. Rep. Steve Magie of Conway was the only Democrat to support the tax cuts.
The bills’ Republican sponsors have said that continuing the yearslong effort to cut taxes is fiscally responsible and will put more money in Arkansans’ pockets.
“This is broad-based tax relief for everyday, working Arkansans,” Searcy Republican Rep. Les Eaves, the House sponsor of the legislation, said before the vote.
Democrats in both chambers echoed concerns expressed Monday by members of the public that the state is choosing not to invest in improvements to public education, childcare, healthcare and agriculture.

Sen. Stephanie Flowers (left), D-Pine Bluff, asks questions about proposed income tax cuts on the Arkansas Senate floor on May 5, 2026. All six Senate Democrats, including Sen. Greg Leding of Fayetteville (center), voted against the measure. All 29 Senate Republicans, including Sen. Terry Rice of Waldron (right) voted for it. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

Medicaid and nutrition assistance are facing steep cuts from the federal government due to the One Big Beautiful Bill measure enacted last year. 
Democratic Sen. Stephanie Flowers asked Republican Sen. Jonathan Dismang, the tax cut measure’s sponsor, if “all the uncertainty and the increases in the federal deficit” make tax cuts an unwise decision.
Dismang said Arkansas has “been very prudent for quite some time with our tax dollars.”
Pearcy Republican Sen. Matt McKee said returning the money to taxpayers was the best way to spend the state’s money.
“What is the best expenditure of that money? I believe it’s putting it back in the hands of the people that produce it,” McKee said.
Arkansas is expected to run a surplus of about $310 million under current law during the upcoming fiscal year, which starts July 1. 
If the new tax rates pass, finance department projections expect a $191.8 million reduction in tax revenue during the fiscal year that begins July 1, and a $144.8 million reduction the following fiscal year.
Democratic Rep. Ashley Hudson of Little Rock, the only House member to speak against the bill, said slashing the top income tax brackets would benefit the wealthy and out-of-state corporations far more than the working families tax cut supporters say the cuts help. 
Hudson cited a list of other needs that could be addressed with the money going toward tax cuts, including food insecurity, maternal mortality, early childhood education and rural healthcare.
The tax cut measures passed days after lawmakers approved spending up to $300 million in incentives for a manufacturer officials hope to lure to West Memphis.
“​​It is not lost on me that over the last month in this room, we have complained about handouts to Arkansans trying to work and care for their children while funding corporate welfare for rich corporations and handouts to out-of-state billionaires who don’t feel it when a gallon of gas gets more expensive,” Hudson said.
Rep. David Ray of Maumelle, speaking in favor of the cuts on the House floor, claimed opponents of the bills who say the cuts would result in programs being underfunded “never define what fully funded means.”
Ray said that Arkansas has invested in maternal health by expanding insurance coverage for low-income mothers, worked to address childhood food insecurity with universal free school breakfast and raised teacher pay. Not cutting taxes doesn’t immediately solve problems, he said.
“The idea that more spending is going to solve all of our problems is ridiculous,” Ray said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Amid extreme drought, New Mexico releases new water dashboard
description: As New Mexico faces extreme drought, the state recently launched a new website to track the state’s water conservation goals.
text:
New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced the release of a website to track the state’s progress on water conservation and creation of new sources. (Photo by GeoSystems Analysis, Inc. courtesy of U.S. Bureau of Reclamation)As New Mexico faces extreme drought, the state recently launched a new website to track the state’s water conservation goals the governor set two years ago.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX
Extremely low snowpack levels threaten the state’s rivers and aquifers this year, a trend that’s expected to continue, with a recent report from water experts across the state projecting that changing climate patterns and groundwater overuse could reduce water supplies by 25% in coming decades. The remaining waters are more vulnerable to pollution concerns from wildfires and other contaminants.
The dashboard includes data on water conservation, development of new water resources and protection of existing water resources, the three elements detailed in Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s 50-year Water Action Plan.
For instance, in the conservation category, the dashboard displays progress on efforts to curb municipal and agricultural demand by 10%. In the expansion arena, it tracks progress on expanding treatment of brackish water to use for non-potable purposes. Lastly, the dashboard sets timelines for protecting existing water supplies through efforts such as restoring watersheds.
“This dashboard is a promise to every New Mexican that we will manage this challenge with the best science available now and well into the future,” Lujan Grisham said in a statement.
Tricia Snyder, the rivers and waters program director for conservation group New Mexico Wild, said the data offers the public more transparency on how the state is going to meet its water goals, by providing information on topics such as aquifer mapping programs, watershed protections and the state’s efforts to take over pollution oversight in its rivers.
“I hope it will be a tool that folks will use as we’re navigating this really tough water year,” Snyder said. “There’s a lot more opportunity to add data points or mapping to it, and I’m excited to work with the governor’s office on how to improve this tool.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: I helped write Colorado’s first AI chatbot bill. Here’s what I learned about state action.
description: For nearly a year, I’ve spent my days on calls with colleagues across the country, researchers, advocates and policy experts all grappling with the same reality: rapidly developing conversational AI technology that we know is doing harm to our communities, an absence of guidelines, and a combination of political and legal challenges that can make […]
text:
(David Espejo/Stock photo via Getty Images)For nearly a year, I’ve spent my days on calls with colleagues across the country, researchers, advocates and policy experts all grappling with the same reality: rapidly developing conversational AI technology that we know is doing harm to our communities, an absence of guidelines, and a combination of political and legal challenges that can make legislation with teeth hard to pass.
I’ve had a front row seat to the work happening in the states on the front lines of the effort to learn the mistakes of the social media era that are now coming home to roost. And I can tell you with confidence, what’s coalescing isn’t a patchwork of regulations, it’s a foundation and a framework that Colorado is learning from and building upon.
The bill that was crafted as a result of those conversations and in partnership with our Colorado legislators, House Bill 26-1263, has now passed the Colorado House and been introduced in the Senate. It would require AI chatbot operators to disclose that users are talking to a machine, follow evidence-based protocols when a user expresses suicidal thoughts or self-harm, and meet stronger standards when their users are minors. It is not a panacea, but rather a critical step forward that Coloradans of all ages, but especially young people, deserve.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX
According to Pew Research, nearly two-thirds of American teenagers report using AI chatbots, and about 1 in 3 use them daily. A nationally representative study found that roughly 5.4 million young Americans have turned to generative AI for mental health advice, and that more than 40 percent of them were never directed toward professional help or crisis resources. In 2025 alone, AI-induced psychosis was linked to multiple suicides and at least one murder.
Colorado kids are the early adopters of this technology, and the risks associated with that adoption are anything by hypothetical. And whatever harms we are tracking today are, almost certainly, the leading edge of something larger.
 


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



I came into this work assuming the state-by-state policy landscape would look chaotic — a patchwork. That’s the word some opponents are using, and to be honest, it’s the word I was bracing for. What I found instead was that California, New York, Oregon, and Washington had each landed on remarkably similar requirements: clear disclosure, protocols for crisis prompts, layered protections for minors. Hawaii and Illinois are moving bills that mirror those same standards. Colorado’s bill was drafted with explicit attention to those frameworks with Colorado-specific adaptations where they were needed.
Some have leveled accusations that this is an “industry bill.” As the person who has been doing the research and work to write the policy behind this legislation, I can tell you that is unequivocally false. The fact that the bill takes frameworks that have passed in other states and builds a Colorado foundation around them isn’t an indication of nefarious intent. It’s an encouraging sign that communities across the country are working to find ways to quickly and effectively meet the moment as AI technology continues to develop so quickly.
It’s also a way to balance Colorado’s needs while managing the “patchwork” concern, which is legitimate. A genuinely fragmented set of laws would create real burdens for compliant companies and real gaps for users who cross state lines. HB-1263 strikes the right balance.
What states are doing right now is about more than filling a gap that Congress will get around to in a few years. It is laying the groundwork for whatever federal framework eventually arrives. And it is doing so along lines that look, from where I’m sitting, more coherent than chaotic.
The bill is part of the movement to design a better future for the next generation; one in which we can embrace the development of AI technology for the potential good it might do, without worrying that every interaction puts users at risk for serious harm.
That, I think, is the story worth telling about HB-1263,  and about every state law like it, working its way through legislatures like ours.
